props.title: They Might Be Giants
props.initialSlug: A quirky romance between a modern Don Quixote & his doc

sections.content: They Might Be Giants stands as a fascinating exploration of mental illness and fantasy through the lens of a Sherlock Holmes-obsessed judge who believes he's the great detective. Like Don Quixote (1972) and The Fisher King (1991), it uses delusion as a gateway to deeper truths. George C. Scott's portrayal of Justin Playfair channels both madness and genius, while Joanne Woodward's Dr. Watson (Dr. Mildred Watson) provides the perfect foil as a psychiatrist gradually pulled into his world. The film predates other notable "reality vs. delusion" classics like Harvey (1950) and King of Hearts (1966).

sections.content: Director Anthony Harvey crafts a unique love letter to both Holmes mythology and New York City itself. The film shares DNA with later works like Midnight Cowboy (1969) and The Taking of Pelham One Two Three (1974) in its gritty yet romantic vision of 1970s New York. The city becomes a character itself, with Playfair treating every street corner as a potential crime scene and every stranger as either a suspect or informant in his imaginary war against Moriarty.

The film's influence can be traced through later works exploring the thin line between genius and madness, from A Beautiful Mind (2001) to Infinitely Polar Bear (2014). Its treatment of mental illness was remarkably progressive for 1971, suggesting that perhaps "sanity" is more fluid than rigid medical definitions would suggest. This theme resonates with later films like Benny & Joon (1993) and Lars and the Real Girl (2007). SUBHEAD: The Holmes Connection

sections.content: While countless films have adapted Sherlock Holmes directly, They Might Be Giants joins works like Without a Clue (1988) and The Seven-Per-Cent Solution (1976) in examining Holmes as a cultural phenomenon. The film's title references Don Quixote's windmill-giants, suggesting that sometimes the "delusional" perspective might offer clearer insight than conventional wisdom.
